title: Climbing Six Flights of Stairs a Day Could Cut Heart Disease Risk, Studies Show
excerpt: A growing body of research finds that taking the stairs daily — even briefly — can meaningfully reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease and premature death.
body:
• A meta-analysis of nine studies involving nearly 500,000 adults found that regular stair climbing was linked to a 24 per cent lower risk of death from any cause and a 39 per cent lower risk of dying from heart disease.
  • About six flights of stairs per day appeared to provide the greatest cardiovascular benefit, though even smaller amounts helped.
  • A separate UK Biobank study of 458,860 adults found that climbing more than five flights daily reduced heart disease risk by up to 20 per cent over 12.5 years.
  • People who stopped climbing stairs during the study period had a 32 per cent higher risk of cardiovascular disease than those who never climbed.

Forget expensive gym memberships and elaborate fitness routines. A growing body of research suggests that one of the most effective things you can do for your heart is already built into most buildings: take the stairs.

A meta-analysis presented at the European Society of Cardiology's Preventive Cardiology conference and recently highlighted in new coverage, pooled data from nine studies involving 480,479 participants aged 35 to 84. The findings were striking: regular stair climbing was associated with a 24 per cent lower risk of dying from any cause and a 39 per cent reduction in cardiovascular mortality.

Climbing about six flights of stairs per day appeared to deliver the greatest benefit, though researchers found that even a few minutes of stair climbing several times per week improved cardiorespiratory fitness and lowered cholesterol.

The UK Biobank Evidence

The meta-analysis builds on a landmark study published in the journal Atherosclerosis, which tracked 458,860 adults from the UK Biobank over a median of 12.5 years. That study found that climbing more than five flights of stairs daily — roughly 50 steps — was associated with a 20 per cent lower risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, including coronary artery disease and ischemic stroke.

The dose-response relationship was clear. Compared with non-stair-climbers, those who climbed six to 10 flights daily had a 7 per cent lower risk. At 11 to 15 flights, the reduction reached 22 per cent. Benefits plateaued at around 20 flights per day.

"Short bursts of high-intensity stair climbing are a time-efficient way to improve cardiorespiratory fitness and lipid profile, especially among those unable to achieve the current physical activity recommendations."

— Dr Lu Qi, Tulane University Obesity Research Center

Perhaps the most sobering finding: participants who had regularly climbed stairs but stopped during the study's five-year resurvey had a 32 per cent higher risk of cardiovascular disease than those who never climbed stairs at all — suggesting that consistency matters more than past effort.

Why Stairs Work

Cardiologists say stair climbing is effective because it functions as both resistance training and cardiovascular exercise simultaneously.

"Stair climbing engages multiple muscle groups, including the quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes, and calves," said Dr Adedapo Iluyomade, a preventive cardiologist at the Miami Cardiac and Vascular Institute. "This type of resistance training can help maintain lean muscle mass, which is crucial for metabolic health and glucose regulation."

The short bursts of high-intensity effort also improve VO2 max — a key marker of cardiovascular efficiency that research has increasingly linked to longevity. And unlike running or cycling, stair climbing is a functional movement that most adults can incorporate into their existing routines without special equipment or dedicated time.

A Practical Option for South Asians

The findings carry particular relevance for South Asian populations, who face a disproportionately high risk of coronary artery disease — often at younger ages and lower BMI thresholds than other ethnic groups. For Indian diaspora professionals working desk-bound jobs, adding stair climbing to the daily commute or office routine offers a no-cost, time-efficient intervention.

Dr Sophie Paddock, the study's lead author from the University of East Anglia, said the research should encourage broader adoption. "Unlike going to the gym or doing a workout, climbing the stairs is something you can easily fit into your day at home, at work or when you're out," she said. "If you have the choice of taking the stairs or the lift, go for the stairs — it will help your heart."

What Researchers Still Want to Know

Scientists have not yet established the precise optimal dose of stair climbing. Future studies using wearable technology are expected to help determine how many flights provide the greatest benefit and at what intensity. For now, the evidence points to a clear conclusion: even modest, consistent stair climbing is one of the simplest interventions available to protect cardiovascular health.
